introduction: “For a single purpose were the Prophets, each and all, sent down to earth.” The guide collects a hundred statements of that purpose: safety and trust among people, the quenching of hatred, the education of souls until divine qualities appear in them, the gathering of scattered flocks, and all of it at the cost of the Messenger’s own suffering and with no claim for himself. Jesus stated his purpose in the same form: “I am come that they might have life”, “to this end was I born”; the Qur’an calls its Prophet a mercy for the peoples and a remembrancer, not a warder; Isaiah and Micah give the picture of peace. The objections are of three kinds. From the scriptures: “I came not to send peace, but a sword”, and “he was wounded for our transgressions”, which makes the mission an atonement and not only an education. From history: Lucretius and Gibbon on what religion has done. From philosophy: Machiavelli on unarmed prophets, Kant on tutelage, Rousseau on the noble origin, Marx on opium, Plato’s rival candidate for the educator of cities.
questions: “I am come that they might have life”; “I came not to send peace, but a sword.” How do the readings account for the division that every Messenger has caused?

Reading 87 says Christ did not come to be believed in or to redeem by his blood. Set out the Christian reading of Isaiah 53 and John 3:16 as a Christian would. Where exactly is the disagreement, and is any of it about words?
Kant wants humanity out of tutelage; the Buddha says you yourself must make the effort. Is the education described in readings 38 to 54 something done to people or with them?
Lucretius and Gibbon judge religion by its history. The readings distinguish the Messengers from their followers. How far does that distinction go, and where does it stop?
“My sole aim hath been to reveal Thee and not my self.” Why do so many of the later readings insist that the Messenger seeks nothing for himself?
Machiavelli says unarmed prophets are destroyed. By what measure do the readings count a prisoner’s mission a success?

outside.why: “For a single purpose were the Prophets, each and all, sent down.” Jesus gathers the law and the prophets into two commandments of love, and says that on these hang all the rest.

“I have come so that” in a world where the door of tranquillity is shut, people may live in safety. Micah: they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree; and none shall make them afraid.
The same sentence-form in John: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly.
The purpose is to summon all to truthfulness, piety and trustworthiness. What doth the Lord require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?

He had no purpose but to quench hatred. Jesus: think not that I am come to send peace on earth: I came not to send peace, but a sword. Every prophet has divided his hearers. How is that fact to be read beside this purpose?
The purpose has been “to forbid conflict, strife”. They shall beat their swords into plowshares; nation shall not lift up sword against nation.

Lucretius, recalling a daughter sacrificed for a fair wind, concluded: so great the evils to which religion could prompt. The reading claims religion’s purpose is to end strife. What must be said about the record he points to?
The purpose of the Kingdom is “the edification of the souls of men”. Till we all come unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ.
“The Appearance of the Manifestations is to bring happiness.” These things have I spoken unto you, that my joy might remain in you, and that your joy might be full.

He sent Messengers and Books that all might live in truth and justice. The Qur’an: We sent Our messengers with clear proofs, and revealed with them the Scripture and the Balance, that mankind may observe right measure.
“We have come to educate the servants.” A messenger of their own, to recite unto them His revelations and to make them grow, and to teach them the Scripture and wisdom.
He came to adorn the world with mercy, “but most of the people do not understand”. He came unto his own, and his own received him not.

“He hath come for the reformation of the world and the life of nations.” Jesus’s own statement of purpose at Nazareth: to preach good tidings to the poor, deliverance to the captives, liberty to them that are bruised.
He Who was promised has come. Many prophets and kings have desired to see those things which ye see, and have not seen them.
“But the people are unaware.” Thou knewest not the time of thy visitation.
“God hath manifested Me for the reformation of the world.” Jesus to Pilate: to this end was I born, and for this cause came I into the world, that I should bear witness unto the truth.

All his life in the hands of his enemies, with no purpose but reform. Machiavelli drew a rule from history: all armed prophets have conquered and the unarmed ones have been destroyed. What kind of success do the readings claim for a prisoner?
He came for the life of the world, and they rose against him. O Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets: how often would I have gathered thy children together, and ye would not!
“He has made the three religions one.” He is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition.

Prophets and sages have all exhorted to unity. The Qur’an: mankind were one community, and God sent prophets as bearers of good tidings and as warners, to judge between mankind in that wherein they differed.
“Specialists of the law of love.” A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you.
The messengers come “with the olive branch of peace and union”. Jesus: I am come to send fire on the earth; and what will I, if it be already kindled? How do the readings account for the fire?
Gibbon set down what was done for centuries under the banner of the cross. The reading speaks of the messengers; he speaks of their followers. Is that distinction enough?
Heavenly Wisdom is eternal peace and universal reconciliation. His name shall be called The Prince of Peace.
God made manifest the true Shepherd to gather all the sheep. Other sheep I have, which are not of this fold; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd.
Ezekiel’s charge against shepherds who feed themselves prepares the promise that God himself will seek his scattered flock.
“The divine Prophets are the true physicians.” They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick.
The mission of the Prophets centres in training. Paul calls the law of Moses a schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ.
They were sent that “the suns of spiritual virtues might shine forth” from human beings. Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.

Through divine education the human world is saved from its darkness. Kant defined enlightenment as man’s release from a tutelage that is his own fault, and bade him use his own understanding without another’s guidance. Is education by a Prophet the tutelage Kant wanted ended, or the means of ending it?
That souls “become manifestations of divine perfections”. That by these ye might be partakers of the divine nature.

“The Prophets are the Educators of men.” Plato looked for the same rescue from another quarter: until philosophers are kings, cities will never have rest from their evils. What can a prophet do that a philosopher cannot?
They come to dispel the darkness of the animal nature. Ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.
That divine qualities may overcome. We all, beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory.
To deliver people “from the slavery of bestial passions”. Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free.
That latent perfections may be brought forth. So God created man in his own image.

The Prophets raise man “from the lowest levels of savagery”. Rousseau told the story the other way: man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains; it is society that corrupts. Which starting-point do the readings need?
Education is the cause of life. Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom.
Prophets come to endow man with virtues. The Buddha: you yourself must make an effort; the Tathagatas are only preachers. How do the readings divide the work between the educator and the educated?
Christ appeared that the image and likeness of God might become manifest in hearts. Paul of Christ himself: who is the image of the invisible God.
Did not Christ live a pure life “as an eternally shining example”? I have given you an example, that ye should do as I have done to you.
They cause the heavenly table to descend. I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger.
When beings are in need He sends teachers. God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets.
Messengers announce “the Straight Path”. Make straight in the desert a highway for our God.
He sent the Messengers for the guidance of His servants. There is not a nation but a warner hath passed among them.
The reading quotes the Qur’an on the Messenger’s duty to convey. A kindred verse: remind them, for thou art but a remembrancer; thou art not at all a warder over them.
“My sole purpose hath been to hand down unto men that which I was bidden.” I can of mine own self do nothing: I seek not mine own will, but the will of the Father which hath sent me.
Since the gate of attainment was closed, He sent holy souls. No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son hath declared him.
“Whoso turns unto them hath turned unto God.” He that believeth on me, believeth not on me, but on him that sent me. And he that seeth me seeth him that sent me.
A testimony to Muhammad’s mission. We sent thee not save as a mercy for the peoples.
Through their advent “the world of existence is renewed”. Behold, I make all things new.
If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.
Prophets enable man to reflect the light. That was the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world.
Each of the eighteen is appointed a mission and sent out. Go ye therefore, and teach all nations.
The Prophets did not come to be worshipped and praised. Peter raises Cornelius: stand up; I myself also am a man.
Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father.

The reading denies that Christ came to be believed in or to redeem by blood. Christians read Isaiah: he was wounded for our transgressions, and with his stripes we are healed. This is the centre of their faith. What would each side need to hear from the other?

For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish. Here belief itself is the stated purpose. Can a mission be both example and atonement?
“I desired naught save to draw people nigh unto God.” I have glorified thee on the earth: I have finished the work which thou gavest me to do.
He has come “to purify you from vain desire”. He shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver.
How could they guide if they had not suffered what others suffer? We have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are.
Educators have to bear enmity and calumny. Socrates describes himself as a gadfly given to the city by God, and expects to be swatted.
They “sacrificed self and forfeited their lives”. He took upon him the form of a servant, and became obedient unto death.

They suffered that humanity might be freed. Marx called religion the sigh of the oppressed creature and the opium of the people: a consolation that keeps the chains on. What in the readings’ account of education and reform would answer him?
“A herald of the Kingdom and a banner of peace.” Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.

“I give sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf.” Jesus’s answer to John’s messengers: the blind receive their sight, the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have the gospel preached to them.
Isaiah had promised it: then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped.
“My sole aim … hath been to reveal Thee and not my self.” Not unto us, O Lord, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory.
“He hath come for the life of the world.” I am the resurrection, and the life.

shortfall: Many of the readings state the purpose of the Manifestation in a single repeated sentence (He hath come for the reformation of the world; the Prophets are sent to educate); companions were given to each form of the statement and not to each repetition.
